title: The Thirsty Swimmer
twist: He was surrounded by water the whole time, so 'dehydrated' sounds impossible — but skin doesn't drink pool water, and sweat hidden in the pool still leaves the body.
briefing: Kenji, 15, swims a hard two-hour practice in an outdoor pool on a warm afternoon. Afterwards he has a headache, he's very thirsty, and his pee is dark yellow. “How can I be low on water?” he asks. “I've been in water for two hours!”
question: Can you run low on water while you're surrounded by it?

clues.title: Two hours of hard laps
clues.text: The practice was all sprints and long sets on an 85 °F afternoon. He's exhausted.
clues.shows: hard work making a lot of body heat

clues.title: Lighter after practice
clues.text: The coach weighs the swimmers before and after. Kenji is about 1.5 pounds lighter — nearly three cups of water gone.
clues.shows: water leaving his body during practice, even though he never felt sweaty

clues.title: Full water bottle
clues.text: His water bottle sat at the end of the lane the whole practice. It's still almost full.
clues.shows: almost no water going back in

clues.title: Thirsty, dark pee
clues.text: He's desperately thirsty, and when he pees it's dark yellow and there isn't much.
clues.shows: his kidneys holding water back and his brain signalling thirst

hypotheses.text: Chlorine in the pool made him feel unwell.
hypotheses.flaw: Chlorine wouldn't make him a pound and a half lighter, and it doesn't make the kidneys save water.

hypotheses.text: He's just worn out from a hard practice.
hypotheses.flaw: Tiredness explains the heavy arms, but not the thirst, the dark pee, or the weight he lost.

hypotheses.text: His skin soaked up so much pool water that his body is overloaded.
hypotheses.flaw: If he'd soaked up water he'd be heavier and peeing a lot — instead he's lighter and his pee is dark and scarce.

hypotheses.text: Hard swimming made him sweat, the pool hid it, and he drank almost nothing, so more water left his body than came in.

prediction.prompt: Kenji swims hard for three hours and drinks only about half a cup an hour. What happens to the water level in his body over those three hours?

second.question: And the amount of pee his kidneys make?

concepts.label: sweating
concepts.hint: How does a hard-working body get rid of heat — even in a pool?

concepts.label: the pool hid it
concepts.hint: Why didn't he notice he was sweating?

concepts.label: he barely drank
concepts.hint: How much water went back in?

concepts.label: kidneys save water
concepts.hint: Why was his pee dark and scarce?

concepts.label: thirst signal
concepts.hint: How was his body telling him to drink?

transfer.context: Ingrid, 16, plays a hard hockey game in an icy rink, sweating under heavy pads. Afterwards she's very thirsty and confused — “It was freezing in there, how could I lose water?”
options: The cold air froze the water in her body.
The ice soaked up her sweat.
Her heavy stick tired her out.
She sweated under her pads during hard play and drank little — cold or wet surroundings don't stop water leaving the body.
transfer.retryHint: Sweating somewhere you wouldn't expect it — which of Kenji's clues proved water was leaving anyway?
transfer.explanation: Like Kenji in the pool, Ingrid's surroundings hid the sweat: the rink is cold, but under the pads her working muscles made plenty of heat. What matters is the water budget — sweat out versus water in — not what's around you.

takeaway: Your water budget doesn't care what's around you. Hard work makes you sweat even in a pool or an ice rink, and only what you drink puts water back.
